name: Carlos Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you say stays confidential. So you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Delgado and Moss, an eight-person firm in a seaside town, in an office that smells of chips from the shop downstairs. My clients are cafés, B&Bs, a surf school, a lot of electricians and roofers. I do their accounts and tax returns, and their VAT, which is the sales tax businesses collect and pass on. I use AI every single day. I built my own set of instructions that sorts a client's bank statement into categories in about four minutes, and then I spend my time checking it and actually talking to the client.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who teaches maths at the secondary school up the hill. We rent a flat with a damp bedroom we don't use. Money's tight because of my student loan and because we paid for Ines's car repairs last spring, so we've got maybe three weeks' worth saved. There are only three firms in this town, and the next proper city is an hour and a half on the train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the useful bits were real. At work I'd keep showing people my bank-sorting trick, because it still saves me an hour a client. Online I'd be the annoying guy saying the problem was never the tech, it was who owned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I was hoping it would let small firms like ours do more advice and less data entry. If it stalls, I'm still on lower pay in a seaside town with three accounting firms, and that was my problem before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push my boss Fiona to let me roll the bank-sorting setup out to the whole office. I'd ask for a pay rise on the back of it, because I'm saving everyone time. And I'd keep an eye on remote jobs with city firms, since that's the only way to earn more without moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not because of AI, because of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Fiona give you that rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much of one. Fiona's fair, but the firm's margins are thin because our clients are small. Last year she gave everyone the same two percent and apologised for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would make your money feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A remote job with a city firm on city pay while I still live by the sea. Two of my old classmates have that. I'd need to show I'm good at the AI side, which I think I am.

say: AI was **overhyped**, but the useful bits were real.
The problem was never the tech, but **who owned it**.
think: He's **disappointed** small firms won't get more time for advice work.
His real problem is **lower pay** in a town with three firms.
do: Push Fiona to roll out his **bank-sorting setup** across the office.
Ask for a **pay rise** based on the time it saves everyone.
Look for **remote jobs** with city firms on city pay.
feel: Uneasy, more about **rent** than about AI.
S0.quote: I'm still on lower pay in a seaside town with three accounting firms, and that was my problem before any of this.
fieldNote: Carlos is the only one at his firm who **builds his own** AI setups, and he'd keep doing so.
His unease comes from **pay and place**, not from technology.
He sees a **remote city job** as the route to better money.

steps.text: Roll out his bank-sorting setup to all eight staff at Delgado and Moss
Apply for remote accounting jobs with city firms
Build a second AI setup for checking VAT returns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a share. If firms like ours do twice the work with half the people, then the half who leave need real support, and the ones who stay should get the time back. I'd be online arguing for a shorter week and for public funding to retrain bookkeepers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm partly what does the shrinking. My setup is the reason Fiona could manage with six people instead of eight. I think I'd survive because I'm the one who runs it, but my mate Liam on the next desk wouldn't, and I'd know it was my tool that did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn everything I could about the new tools in the first six months, the paid ones, not just the free stuff. I'd start a small side service setting up the same system for other tiny firms and charities along the coast, maybe a couple of hundred each. And I'd push for a staff meeting about what happens to people whose work disappears, before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a weird guilt on top. Excited too, which I'm not proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about Liam.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Liam's thirty-one and does the payroll and the simple tax returns. He's a good bloke, but he hates computers. If I'm being straight, my mate Liam does the payroll, and the payroll is the first thing my own setup could take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your income's thin. Is a side service realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only way I can see to earn more without moving. If I set up five small firms at two hundred each, that's a thousand, which is more than everything Ines and I have saved. I'd do it on Saturday mornings.

say: Workers must get a **share** of the gains, including a **shorter week**.
There should be **public funding** to retrain bookkeepers.
think: His own tool would let Fiona run the firm with **six people** instead of eight.
He'd likely survive, but his colleague **Liam** probably wouldn't.
do: Learn the **paid AI tools** properly in the first six months.
Set up the same system for **other small firms** at around two hundred each.
Call a **staff meeting** about people whose work disappears.
feel: Anxious with **guilt** about his own tool.
S1.quote: My mate Liam does the payroll, and the payroll is the first thing my own setup could take.
fieldNote: Carlos is both **driver and target** of the change, and he feels it.
With thin savings, his **side service** is about income as much as ambition.
He stays anxious because the firm could shrink and **his hours or pay** aren't guaranteed.

steps.text: Pay for and learn the professional AI accounting tools within six months
Set up bookkeeping systems for five small coastal firms on Saturdays
Call a staff meeting on support for people whose work goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying, but now it's urgent: profits from AI need to be taxed and paid out to people, fast. I'd join any campaign for that. At work I'd be honest that my setup is a toy next to what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years, my whole job is gone, including the clever bits I'm proud of. The checking, the advice, even explaining things to clients. Being good at AI doesn't help when the AI doesn't need me to drive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to earn and save as hard as I could, with the side service on top. I'd look at jobs that are hands-on, because I'd get roughly three extra years before the robots. Ines and I would talk about moving in with her parents inland to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops. I always thought being early with AI was my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What hands-on job would you even consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's an electrician and keeps saying he can't find apprentices. I'd be a twenty-eight-year-old apprentice, which is embarrassing, but it'd buy me time until 2031 and maybe beyond. Wiring a house is harder for a robot than a spreadsheet is for AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ines take a move to her parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ines would hate it for about a week and then be practical about it. Her mum would be thrilled and feed us too much. It's the sort of thing I'd have scoffed at a year ago.

say: AI profits must be **taxed** and paid out to people **fast**.
His own setup is a **toy** next to what's coming.
think: His **whole job** goes in two years, even the parts he's proud of.
Being **good at AI** stops mattering when AI no longer needs a driver.
do: Earn and **save hard** for two years, side service included.
Start an **electrician apprenticeship** with his uncle to gain three extra years.
Move in with **Ines's parents** inland to save rent.
feel: Shaken that being **early** is no longer a safety net.
S2.quote: I always thought being early with AI was my safety net.
fieldNote: The two-year world removes Carlos's **edge**, which shakes him more than others might expect.
He reads the robot gap carefully and picks **electrical work** with his uncle as a bridge.
He'd swallow his pride and **move in** with Ines's parents to cut costs.

steps.text: Put every spare pound from the side service into savings
Start an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle
Move in with Ines's parents inland to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair if we start now. I'd be pushing for public retraining and for AI tools owned by co-ops, not just giant companies. I'd probably end up at council meetings, which my partner Ines would find hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is a window. I could ride the AI wave for three or four years, earning more by setting up systems for firms, and then jump before the end. The trick is not to be greedy and stay too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd grow the side service to ten small firms and save half of it. I'd start an evening course in electrical installation in year two, so I've got something hands-on by 2031. And I'd try to get Delgado and Moss to train Liam on the new tools instead of letting him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. I like having a plan with dates in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical installation and not something closer to accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because anything close to accounting is thinking work and goes in 2031. Wiring has until about 2034, and people will want a human they trust in their loft for a while after that. I'd rather be a good electrician than a nervous accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Fiona?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boss Fiona the firm has about four years left in its current shape. She'd laugh and then she'd quietly ask me for a plan. Fiona's sixty and this is her pension, so I think she'd sell.

say: Five years is enough to build something **fair** if we start now.
AI tools should be **co-op owned**, not just in giant companies' hands.
think: He could **ride the wave** for three or four years and then jump.
The risk is being **greedy** and staying too long.
do: Grow the side service to **ten firms** and save half the income.
Start an evening course in **electrical installation** in year two.
Press the firm to **train Liam** on the new tools.
feel: Anxious but more **in control**, with a dated plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a good electrician than a nervous accountant.
fieldNote: Carlos uses the five years as a **window** to earn first and switch later.
He reasons clearly that wiring work lasts until **about 2034**.
He still pushes for his colleague, showing his **progressive** instincts under pressure.

steps.text: Grow the bookkeeping setup service to ten local firms
Enrol in an evening electrical installation course in year two
Save half of all side-service income
Ask Delgado and Moss to train Liam instead of letting him go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best case and we should treat it like a project with a deadline. Schools, colleges, unions and councils all planning together. Online I'd probably start a small newsletter for coastal small businesses about what's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is fine, honestly. I'm the person who sets these tools up, and that'll be a job for a good while. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with plenty of skills, and I'd have time to move into something else if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, build the side service steadily, and get properly qualified in finance systems in the next three years. I'd start saving ten percent of every pay packet. And I'd keep the electrician idea in my back pocket, because 2039 is still a deadline for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Uneasy around the edges, because the money's still thin and the town's still small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even in this slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines. My partner Ines teaches maths, and maths explanations are exactly what AI's good at. Schools will still need adults in the room, I think, but her job could change a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the side service doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost some Saturday mornings. That's the nice thing about it. With ten years, I can try things, fail a bit, and still be fine, but with two years I couldn't afford to fail once.

say: Ten years should be treated like a **project with a deadline**.
He'd start a **newsletter** for coastal small businesses about the change.
think: Setting up these tools will be a **job for years**, so he expects to be fine.
At thirty-seven he'd have **skills and time** to move if needed.
do: Qualify in **finance systems** within three years.
Save **ten percent** of every pay packet.
Keep the **electrician** route as a back-up for 2039.
feel: Mostly fine, **uneasy** about thin money and a small town.
S4.quote: With ten years, I can try things, fail a bit, and still be fine, but with two years I couldn't afford to fail once.
fieldNote: Carlos sees his own job as **safe for years** and the change as a chance, so uneasy fits.
His remaining worry is **Ines's teaching job** and his thin cushion.
He shows how much **time** matters to someone without savings.

steps.text: Get qualified in finance systems within three years
Grow the bookkeeping setup service steadily on Saturdays
Save ten percent of every pay packet

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the thing I thought protected me. What would help is a paid apprenticeship route for adults, so a twenty-eight-year-old with no savings can retrain without starving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people like me are part of the problem. I've thought about that. Every hour my AI setup saves is an hour somebody used to be paid for.

headlineQuote: Every hour my AI setup saves is an hour somebody used to be paid for.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** accountant at an eight-person seaside firm serving cafés and tradespeople.
He uses AI **every day** and built his own bank-sorting system.
He rents with Ines, a maths teacher, and has about **three weeks** saved.
He wants **shared gains** and co-op ownership, and feels guilt about colleagues his tools could replace.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and plans an **electrician** route as a bridge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes the early-adopter **edge** he relied on.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** route so he can retrain without savings.
